topics.title: Kalki's king and a tiger prophecy

learn.hook: A ten-day-old baby sits up and lectures the royal astrologers. From that moment, you know this story is a satire.
points: Author: Kalki, the pen name of R. Krishnamurthy, a Tamil writer and journalist known for satire.
Type: a satire on the vanity of rulers and on the destruction of wildlife.
Hero: Maharaja Sir Jilani Jung Jung Bahadur of Pratibandapuram, known as the Tiger King.
At his birth the astrologers foretold that he would one day die because of a tiger.
The ten-day-old prince miraculously spoke and warned that tigers should beware: a deliberately absurd, exaggerated moment.

example.q: Why does the author include the talking ten-day-old prince?
steps: A baby cannot really speak at ten days.
The absurd miracle mocks the grand myths built around royals.
It sets a humorous, satirical tone.
example.answer: To exaggerate and mock royal legends, setting up the story's satire.

learn.reallife: Wildlife officials in India say many tigers were lost to royal hunts in the princely era. Kalki's satire hits a real target.

topics.title: The vow of a hundred tigers

learn.hook: Told that a tiger may kill him, the king decides to kill tigers first, a hundred of them.
points: The prince was raised the 'English' way: an English nurse (nanny) and an English tutor. At twenty he became king.
He killed his first tiger and vowed to kill a hundred. The chief astrologer warned him: he might kill ninety-nine, but he must be careful with the hundredth.
To keep all the tigers for himself, he banned tiger hunting by anyone else in his state.

example.q: Why did the Maharaja ban tiger hunting by others?
steps: He had vowed to kill a hundred tigers himself.
Others hunting would reduce the number left for him.
So he made tiger hunting his own monopoly.
example.answer: To keep all the tigers for himself so he could complete his vow of a hundred kills.

learn.reallife: Today India's Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, bans tiger hunting for everyone, kings included. Kalki's Maharaja banned it only so he could hunt alone.

topics.title: Diamonds for a duchess, brides for tigers

learn.hook: To keep his tigers, the king risks his throne. To keep his throne, he buys diamonds. To find more tigers, he chooses a wife.
points: A high-ranking British officer wanted to hunt a tiger in the state. The king refused, and risked losing his throne.
He saved his kingdom by sending about fifty costly diamond rings to the officer's wife, who chose one or two but kept them all.
Within ten years he had killed seventy tigers, and tigers vanished from his state.
He then married a girl from a state with many tigers, and killed tigers there on each visit to his father-in-law.

example.q: What does the Maharaja's choice of bride reveal about him?
steps: He chooses her for her state's tiger population.
Marriage becomes a tool for his vow.
His obsession rules even his personal life.
example.answer: That his obsession with killing tigers is so great that even his marriage is chosen to serve it.

learn.reallife: Bribery to stay in power is an old target of satire. Kalki's fifty diamond rings make the point through comic exaggeration.

topics.title: The hundredth tiger takes its revenge

learn.hook: Ninety-nine down. The last tiger is an old one from a park, and the king's bullet misses. The real hundredth tiger is made of wood.
points: After ninety-nine tigers, none were left. The worried dewan secretly brought an old tiger from the People's Park in Madras and let it loose.
The king's bullet missed. The tiger fainted from shock; the hunters found it alive and killed it secretly, without telling the king.
For his son's third birthday, the king bought a cheap wooden toy tiger, crudely carved. A sliver from it pierced his right hand.
The infection spread; he died during the operation. The hundredth tiger had taken its revenge.

steps: The king believes he has killed his hundredth tiger, but it was actually killed by hunters.
The real 'hundredth' tiger is the wooden toy.
A sliver from it causes the infection that kills him.
example.answer: The wooden toy tiger, effectively the hundredth, wounds him and leads to his death, as the astrologer foretold.

learn.reallife: Doctors in India warn that even a small wooden splinter can cause a serious infection if ignored. Kalki uses this tiny cause for a huge, ironic end.

topics.title: The Maharaja, the dewan and the astrologer

learn.hook: A vain king, a frightened but clever minister, and an astrologer who gets the last laugh.
points: The Maharaja: vain, stubborn and proud of his power; he risks his throne, bribes officials and wipes out tigers for his vow.
The dewan: fearful of the king but cunning; he smuggles in an old tiger to save his own job.
The chief astrologer: prophetic; his warning about the hundredth tiger comes true.
Theme: satire on royalty, arrogance and the abuse of power.

example.q: How does the dewan show both fear and cunning?

learn.reallife: Political satire in India, from R.K. Laxman's cartoons to modern sketches, pokes fun at the vanity of the powerful, the same target as Kalki's.

learn.hook: The man who killed ninety-nine real tigers dies because of a wooden one. Irony doesn't get sharper than that.
points: Irony of fate and the inevitability of destiny: the king tries to defeat the prophecy, but it is fulfilled in an unexpected way.
Destruction of wildlife: one man's vanity wipes out tigers from his state and beyond; the story indirectly argues for conservation.
Satire, irony and dramatic irony: readers know the 'hundredth' tiger was killed by hunters while the king celebrates.
Humour and exaggeration (a talking baby, fifty rings, a bride chosen for tigers), with suspense around the hundredth tiger.

example.q: Explain the dramatic irony in the hunt of the old tiger.

learn.hook: Vow, rings, toy tiger: three short answers. Irony and satire: one long answer. Let's lock them in.
points: Irony builds suspense: we wait for the hundredth tiger, sure it will be dangerous, and the danger comes from a toy.
Satire on those in power: vanity, bribery (the rings), selfish bans, and a ruler who thinks he can defeat fate.
Wildlife: the story shows how hunting for pride wiped out tigers; it supports conservation by showing the cost.
The vow leads to death: the obsession with a hundred tigers leads to the toy that kills him.
Short answers on the vow, the rings and the toy tiger; long answer on irony and satire.

example.q: Write a 50-word answer: How does the Maharaja's vow lead to his death?
steps: The vow: kill a hundred tigers to defeat the prophecy.
The 99th and the fake 100th leave him confident.
The wooden toy becomes the real hundredth tiger; its sliver kills him.
example.answer: To defeat the prophecy, the Maharaja vowed to kill a hundred tigers. Believing he had killed the hundredth, he relaxed. But the wooden toy tiger he bought for his son became the true hundredth; its sliver caused a fatal infection.

learn.reallife: Satire like Kalki's appears in Indian newspapers' editorial cartoons every day. Learning to spot it in literature helps you spot it in life.
